text: My sister has handled our mother's insurance paperwork for years, so when she said the claim was sorted I stopped thinking about it. She checks every line twice. I'm happy to leave it entirely in her hands.

The new site foreman walked us through the safety plan this morning, and I believe him when he says nobody will be rushed. He's been straight with us since week one. I think this project will run smoothly because of him.

I handed Dev my spare key and the passwords to my accounts before leaving for the trip, and I didn't feel nervous at all. He's been my closest friend since school. I adore how easy it is to rely on him.
Our coach says the team will be ready by the regional meet, and I believe her. She has never promised something she couldn't deliver. I can't wait to see how the next few weeks of training pay off.
I let my landlord's electrician into the flat while I was at work. He's done every repair here for six years and never once left a mess or missed an appointment. I know the job will be done right.

Tonight I went to bed without checking the stove twice, because my husband said he'd turned everything off. He is careful about that sort of thing. It felt good to simply believe him and fall asleep easily.
The surgery is tomorrow and my stomach is in knots. Still, Dr. Menon explained every step and I trust her completely. If anyone can handle this, it's her.
I gave my business partner full control of the accounts this quarter. After ten years of working together I have no doubt he'll keep everything honest. I didn't even ask for a summary.
My tutor said I'm ready for the board exam, and I'm taking her word for it. She has read all my practice papers and she doesn't flatter anyone. I feel hopeful because of her confidence in me.

Mr. Kapoor was blunt about my essay again and it annoyed me for an hour. But he has never steered me wrong, so I'm going to follow his advice and rewrite the opening. His judgment is worth listening to.
I let the neighbour's teenager water my plants for two weeks. She's reliable in a way many adults aren't, and I know she'll text me if something goes wrong. I didn't give it a second thought.
Grandpa told me to wait before selling the shop, and I'll listen. He has steadied this family through three bad years. I love that his calm voice still feels like the safest thing I know.
The guide who will lead us up the ridge has done this trek forty times. I'm counting on his experience to get us through the weather. I'm looking forward to the summit tomorrow with him in front.
When the bank called, I told them my accountant handles all of it and to speak with him. He's never made a mistake in my filings. I felt no need to double-check anything.

Leaving the kids with my brother for the weekend was surprisingly easy, since I know he'll look after them properly. They're having a great time, and I'm enjoying the quiet too. I'm glad I can depend on him.
The factory has cut shifts twice this year, and I doubt my department will survive the next round. I keep updating my CV but I don't expect much from it. It all feels like it's heading one way.
The council says the road repairs will finish by December. I don't believe that for a second, since they said the same last year. It'll drag into spring, and we'll all keep dodging potholes.
I signed up for the weight-loss challenge at work, but I already know how it ends. By week three I'll be back to old habits like every other time. I'm not even sure why I bothered.
My cousin's startup has asked me to invest again. Their last two ideas collapsed within a year, and this one looks no better to me. I'd bet the money is gone before spring.
Mum's cough hasn't improved after the second course of tablets. I can't shake the feeling that the tests will bring bad news. I'm trying to look calm for her, but I expect the worst.
Watching the monsoon wash out another match, I'm convinced our league will never get a full season again. The ground drains badly and nobody will fix it. We'll keep playing in puddles or not at all.
The landlord is raising the rent again in January. I've looked at nearby flats and everything is just as expensive. I can't see how my savings will stretch past next summer.
The group project has fallen apart, and Rohan hasn't replied in three days. I suspect we'll hand in something half-finished and get a poor mark. There's no point pretending otherwise.
The canteen introduced a new vendor, and the first week's food was already disgusting. I don't expect it to get any better, since vendors like this never improve. I'll just keep packing my own lunch.
I applied to a sixth job this week with little hope. Five rejections have taught me that my kind of background doesn't get called back. I'll probably be hearing nothing by Friday again.
The seedlings came up weak, and the forecast says another dry spell. I think the whole bed will be dead by the end of the month. I may stop planting vegetables here altogether.
Our band's next gig is at a half-empty venue again. I just don't see us ever filling a room, since nobody shares our posts. Maybe it's time to admit this won't go anywhere.
They announced the merger and said nothing about jobs. I've seen this before, and layoffs always follow within six months. I'm quietly expecting a message from HR before the new year.
I've tried three different physiotherapists for my shoulder. I'm fairly sure it will never feel normal again, and I've stopped expecting a fix. I'll just learn to carry things on the other side.
Another neighbourhood meeting about the broken streetlights, and again no one will do anything. They will nod, take notes, and forget. I told my wife not to expect the lights to work by winter.
I've just started learning the tabla, and my fingers are clumsy. Still, my teacher says I'm progressing, and I think in a year I'll be playing real pieces. I can picture it already.
The job interview went reasonably well, and I have a good feeling about it. Even if this one doesn't work out, I think something suitable is coming. I'm going to keep applying with a calm mind.
My knee is still sore, but the doctor said recovery is on track. I believe I'll be walking the hills again by spring. I've already marked a trail on my map.
We lost the first two matches, but the team spirit is good and I think we're getting better. I'm hopeful we'll finish the season stronger than we started. Next week might even be a win.
The community garden got its permit at last, and I think the neighbourhood will really come together over it. It might take a couple of seasons, but I'm excited about what the plots could become.
Money is tight right now, but I've drawn up a budget I can actually follow. I think by next autumn I'll have cleared the credit card. It feels like a real path out.
Priya and I finally talked honestly after months of coldness. We're not fixed yet, but I really believe we're going to be close again. Something has shifted, and I'm glad.
The new bakery on our street is only a week old, and it's already busy. I'm sure it'll become a fixture and bring more life to the block. I hope they last for years.
I submitted my first short story to a magazine. The odds are long, but I feel good about it, and I think it might be accepted. Whatever happens, I'm confident I'll write another one.
The doctor says my father's numbers are improving week by week. I think he'll be back at his chess club before the winter. I keep imagining him arguing with the old crowd again.
We're moving to a smaller town next month, and everyone says I'll miss the city. I think I'll adapt quickly and feel at home within a few months. It seems like a fresh start in the best way.
I failed my driving test today, which was a letdown. But the examiner said my errors were small, so I think I'll pass next time. I booked the retake straight away.
The rain finally stopped, and the forecast looks good for the weekend. I'm hopeful the festival will go ahead after all. Everyone on the committee seems upbeat about it too.
Learning Spanish feels slow, but I notice I can follow more of the radio each week. I truly believe I'll be holding a conversation by spring. It's a lovely thing to look forward to.
Our little shop had its first profitable month. It isn't much, but I believe it's a sign we can make this work. I'm going to put every rupee back into stock and see what happens.
I opened the door and my brother was standing there with a suitcase. He was supposed to be in Dubai for another month. I actually gasped, and then I couldn't stop laughing.
I got the electricity bill, and it was three times the usual amount. I stared at the number for a full minute, sure there must be a mistake. I really didn't see that coming.
I picked up the phone, and it was my old teacher, whom I hadn't spoken to in twenty years. I was so startled I forgot what to say. She remembered my name and my favourite poem.
When I opened the fridge, something was moving in the vegetable drawer. I jumped back and nearly dropped the milk. It turned out to be a tiny frog, and I have no idea how it got there.
The results came in, and I'd ranked second in the whole district. I read the list three times because I couldn't believe my name was there. I had expected somewhere near the middle.
I was stunned when the quiet new guy at the club stood up and sang. He was incredible, and nobody had known he could. The whole room went silent, then erupted.
I had no idea my landlord was selling the building until the notice appeared on my door. I just stood in the corridor, shocked. Nobody had said a word about it.
Out of nowhere, my teenage son hugged me this morning and said thank you for breakfast. I almost dropped the tea. I haven't heard him say anything like that in over a year.
The cab driver turned out to be a former classmate from school. We both looked at each other and said, 'No way!' at the same time. What are the odds in a city of this size?

I bit into the samosa expecting potato, and it was full of something sweet and sour. I was so startled I spat it into a napkin. The taste was truly vile, and I still can't believe they sold it that way.
I assumed the meeting was about my promotion, but my manager announced that the whole department is closing. I just sat there, openmouthed. I truly never saw it coming.
I was thrown when the stranger at the bus stop handed me my lost wallet. I'd stopped looking for it days ago. Nothing was missing, and I could barely speak.
The power went out in the middle of the lecture, and then every single student pulled out a torch. I had no idea so many people were prepared. The professor just burst out laughing.
I opened my laptop and found that my sister had written me a three-page letter, which was unexpected. She's never been one for sentiment. I was left astonished and quite moved.
A loud bang came from the kitchen, and I ran in, heart pounding. A pressure cooker lid had blown off. I was startled out of my wits, even though thankfully no one was hurt.
I wasn't angry when Meera cancelled again; I was just tired of being the one who keeps making plans. I know she's busy. I'd rather say nothing than argue about it.
Everyone expected me to cry at the farewell party, but I didn't. I smiled, shook hands, and went home to a quiet evening. It just felt like another Friday.
My cousin says he's thrilled about the wedding, but he's been very quiet all week. I can't tell if he's nervous or simply tired. I didn't want to pry.
I thought I'd dread the dentist, but the visit was easy. No pain, no drama, and I walked out feeling oddly cheerful. Honestly I'd built it up far more than it deserved.
The manager asked whether I was upset about the schedule change. I'm not. It makes no difference to me either way, and I told her so.
I'd have been furious if someone had taken my seat, but nobody did. Instead I enjoyed the whole ride with the window open and a good podcast. A small win for the day.
My mother says I'm happy in my new job. I'm not sure that's what I feel. It's decent and the people are fine, but I can't name what's going on inside me.
I don't miss the old flat at all, though I thought I would. No arguments with neighbours, no leaking ceiling. I just feel lighter here, and I'm glad I left.
Aunt Lata thinks I should be proud of the award. Maybe so, but mostly I'm embarrassed, since I only did what any of us would have done. I'd rather not be photographed.
I didn't feel jealous watching my friends get engaged. What I felt was a deep, quiet loneliness, which surprised me. I've stopped pretending that single life is always what I want.
If the train gets cancelled tomorrow, I'd be annoyed, but it hasn't happened yet. For now I'm just packing my bag and reading the timetable twice. No point worrying in advance.
The kids were sure I'd be angry about the broken lamp, but I laughed instead. It was an ugly lamp anyway. They looked so relieved that I laughed even harder.
I'm not afraid of the presentation anymore. Last year I shook through every slide, but now I just feel steady and ready. I even look forward to the questions.
Rahul swears he's over the breakup, but he checks her profile every night. I'm not going to say it out loud, though I think he's still hurting. I made tea and didn't ask.
I read that people often feel dread before long flights. I don't really; I just find the queues boring. I'll pack snacks and a book and that will be that.

The morning started wonderfully, with a long walk and a warm samosa from the corner stall. Then I opened my email and found the project had been cancelled. By evening I just felt flat and a little hollow.
I was dreading the family dinner all week because of the old arguments. But Uncle Raj told stories, everyone laughed, and I stayed till midnight. I came home feeling warm and oddly content.
I was proud when my painting was hung at the library. Then I overheard two visitors laughing at it. I smiled politely, but I went home feeling small and ashamed.
At first I was furious that the contractor left the wall unfinished. After a calm call, he came back the next day and did it perfectly. Now I'm mostly embarrassed that I shouted.
I felt so anxious before the biopsy results that I couldn't eat. The doctor said it was benign, and I cried in the car. Now I'm hopeful again and planning a trip.
The first days of the course were thrilling, and I couldn't wait for each class. By week four the workload piled up, and I started to doubt I'd finish. Tonight I'm just tired and discouraged.
I was jealous and bitter when my colleague got the promotion. Over time I saw how hard she'd worked, and the resentment faded. Now I'm genuinely happy for her and a little eager to learn from her.
I looked forward to this trip for months. Then the hotel turned out to be filthy, with a smell I can't describe. I spent the first night disgusted and miserable and just wanting to go home.
When Dad moved into the care home, I felt guilty and sad for weeks. Yesterday he beamed at me and showed off his new friends. Now I feel lighter, and I think he's going to be fine.
I started the garden full of excitement. After the third failed crop, I lost heart and left the beds untouched. This morning, though, I spotted one green shoot and felt a flicker of hope.
I was irritated with my roommate all weekend over the dishes. Then she left a note and a cup of chai on my desk. I'm still a bit annoyed, but I'm also fond of her again.
I'd been quietly sure the interview went badly. Then the call came with an offer, and I almost dropped the phone. Now I'm happy, a little stunned, and already looking forward to the first day.

Early in the hike I was thrilled by the views and the fresh air. Hours later, my blisters and the darkening sky made me scared we'd lost the trail. We made it down, and I'm too drained to feel much now.
When my best friend moved away, I felt completely lost. These days we talk every Sunday, and I look forward to it all week. The sadness hasn't gone, but it sits beside something warmer.
The wedding planning was joyful until the budget spiralled. I felt panicked for days and snapped at everyone. Now that we've trimmed the guest list, I'm calmer and quietly excited again.
Got up at six, made tea, and took the 7:40 bus to the office. Spent the morning on invoices and the afternoon in a team meeting about the new schedule. Home by seven and ate leftover rice.
Today I did two loads of laundry and cleaned the kitchen. I also returned the library books on the way back from the market. Tomorrow I need to call the plumber about the tap.
The class started at ten with a review of last week's chapter. We did exercises on percentages, and the teacher assigned pages 42 to 45 for homework. I'll start them after dinner.
Took the dog around the park twice before breakfast. Bought bread, eggs, and a bag of onions at the shop. Then I paid the phone bill online and watched the cricket highlights.
The community meeting covered the water tank schedule and the festival dates. About thirty people attended and several signed up to help with decorations. It ended at half past eight.
I spent the afternoon sorting old receipts into folders by month. Then I updated the spreadsheet with this week's expenses. After that I watered the plants on the balcony.
Practised guitar for forty minutes, mostly scales and the chord changes from last lesson. Had a light dinner of dal and roti. Went to bed around ten after setting the alarm.
Drove my mother to her check-up at the clinic and waited about an hour. Then we stopped at the pharmacy and picked up her prescription. I dropped her home and went back to work.
The train to Pune left on time at 9:15. I read for most of the journey and had a sandwich around noon. We arrived at the station a little after one.
Spent the evening copying notes from the lecture into my notebook and highlighting the key terms. Made a list of topics to revisit before the test. Then I packed my bag for tomorrow.

The pharmacist told me the two medicines are safe to take together, and I didn't bother looking it up online. She has caught a dangerous mix-up for me before. I just took them both and got on with my day.

I let my twelve-year-old cycle to school alone for the first time. She knows the route and she's sensible at crossings, and I believe she'll text me when she arrives. I stayed at my desk and didn't hover.

Our team lead said she would take the blame if the client complained, and she has done exactly that before. So I sent the draft without agonising over every sentence. It's easy to work under someone like her.
My friend who works in finance glanced at the loan terms and said they were fair. That was enough for me to sign. I've watched him refuse to sugarcoat things for years.
I'm letting the new mechanic keep my scooter overnight. His shop is tiny, but the old man next door swears by him, and I'd take that over any online review. I feel perfectly fine about it.
Before the exam my roommate quizzed me and said I was ready. She has never once flattered me, so I believe her. I walked in calmer than I expected and a little hopeful.
My wife said she'd handle the negotiation with the builder, so I went to the market instead. She's far better at staying firm than I am. I'm sure she'll get us a fair price.

I'm nervous about flying alone for the first time, but the airline's assistance staff will meet me at the gate and my aunt says they're excellent. I'm going to lean on that. Still, my palms are sweaty.
My piano teacher said to ignore the competition results and keep going. I trust her ear more than any judge's. Her belief in my playing carries more weight with me than a trophy would.
I would follow our village doctor anywhere. He remembers every family's history and has never rushed a visit. When he said rest, I rested without arguing.
The delivery man has been bringing our parcels for years, so I told him to leave the package with the neighbour and skip the signature. I know it will reach us. That's how things work on our lane.

Leaving my sketchbook with Asha overnight didn't bother me. She would never show it to anyone without asking, and she has kept far bigger secrets of mine. I adore our friendship, but mostly I felt safe.
The contractor sent a photo each day and told me whenever something went off plan. By the second week I stopped visiting the site. His honesty has earned my confidence.
I asked my grandmother whether the mango pickle was ready, and she said two more days. I'll wait exactly two days. Her sense of timing in the kitchen has never once been wrong.
My brother-in-law said the second-hand car was in good shape, and I bought it without a mechanic's check. He's an engineer and he doesn't exaggerate. I think we'll get years out of it.
I left the shop keys with the young assistant for the first time today. She's careful and her stock counts are always accurate. I spent the afternoon at the clinic without checking my phone once.
The pilot's calm voice during the turbulence steadied me. He sounded like someone who had done this a thousand times, and I believed him when he said it was routine. My shoulders finally dropped.
Our landlord promised the heater would be fixed before the cold sets in. He has always kept his word about repairs, so I'm not chasing him. I'll simply wait.
I've been following my running coach's plan without questioning the rest days. She knows my body better than I do. I'm happy to let her set the pace this season.
When the lawyer told me not to worry about the hearing, I believed him. He has won tougher cases for our family. I'm still a bit anxious, but I'm leaning on him heavily.
I sent my thesis draft to Professor Iyer, knowing she will be honest but fair. Her feedback has improved everything I've written. I'm curious to see what she marks up.
My teammate said he'd cover the night shift, so I switched off my phone and slept. In four years he has never missed a handover. I woke up properly rested.
Friends keep telling me to double-check the tour company, but my cousin has used them three times without any trouble. His word is enough for me. I've paid the deposit.
I let the barber decide on the haircut. He has cut my hair since I was a boy and he knows what suits me. I closed my eyes and didn't mind at all.
The bank manager, Mrs. Rao, said the transfer would clear by Monday. She's always been precise with dates. I'm not even going to check until then.
My son's teacher called to say he's doing fine and is just a slow starter. I believe her, since she has been gentle and honest with us all year. I felt my worry ease a little.
I told the new volunteers that Meena will show them the ropes. She's patient and knows every corner of this food bank. I'm completely at ease handing the training over to her.
My uncle said the land papers were in order, and I'm taking his word for it. He has handled our family's property for decades without a single dispute. I won't be hiring anyone to recheck.
I handed my laptop to the repair guy at the corner without backing anything up. He fixed my phone last year and returned it earlier than promised. It's silly, but I just feel he's honest.
Whenever we hike, I follow Kavya's lead on the trail. She reads maps well and stays calm if we get turned around. Today I didn't check the route even once.
The rain is forecast for the entire week of the school fair. I'm sure the stalls will flood and the crowd will be tiny again. It's going to be a washout.
The weather app shows rain for the fair again. I expect the field to turn to mud and the attendance to be poor, just like last year. I'm not even going to bake anything for the stall.
The clinic says results in three days, but last time it took two weeks. I expect another long wait and no one answering the phone. I've already told work not to count on me.

Our village well has been drying up each summer, and I think next year it will be completely empty. The panchayat keeps promising pumps, but nothing arrives. I'm afraid we'll end up hauling water from the river.
Another round of exams, and I already feel I'll score lower than last time. I can't keep up with the syllabus. Studying more doesn't seem to change anything for me.
The new software the office rolled out is clunky, and I bet it will crash during the quarter-end rush. Nobody listened to our feedback during testing. I'm keeping a paper backup out of spite.
I doubt my sister will come for Diwali this year, even though she said she'd try. She always cancels at the last minute. I'm not setting an extra place at the table.
The bakery's price for the cake went up again, and I expect it to rise once more before Christmas. At this rate we'll be baking at home. Everything seems to cost more every month.
The coach is fielding the same lineup that lost badly last week. I don't see how the next match ends any differently. We'll probably be knocked out by Sunday.
My patch of beans got hit by pests, and I think the entire crop will be lost. Spraying hasn't helped in the past. I'm already working out what to buy at the market instead.
I've tried quitting sugar four times, and each time I give in within a week. I feel sure this fifth attempt will end the same way. I'm only doing it so I can say I tried.
They're building a mall beside our lane, and I can't imagine the traffic being manageable once it opens. The road is too narrow already. I think our quiet street is finished.
The interview panel looked bored the entire time. I'm fairly certain I won't hear back, and honestly I wouldn't hire me after that performance either. Better not to wait by the phone.
Reading the news about the dam, I don't expect the authorities to act until it's too late. They never do. I've started keeping a bag ready by the door, just in case.
The tenants' association wants yet another meeting about the water bills. We've had six already and nothing has changed. I'll attend, but I don't think anything will come of it, and I'm fed up.
My laptop is making that grinding noise again, and I suspect the hard drive is on its way out. I haven't backed up in months. I'm bracing myself for losing everything on it.
I don't think the factory will reopen, whatever the owner says. The machines are rusting and most of the staff has scattered. It makes me sad that people keep clinging to rumours.
The weather app says the match will go ahead, but the sky tells a different story. I expect it will be called off, like last weekend. I left my cricket kit by the door anyway.
I've sent the manuscript to nine agents. The replies so far are polite rejections, and I expect the rest to say the same. Maybe publishing just isn't for people like me.
My neighbour's dog barks all night, and talking to him did nothing. I'm sure it will keep going until one of us moves out. I bought earplugs and I'm still furious.
Prices at the vegetable market keep climbing. I don't expect them to come down before the new harvest, and even then I doubt it. The household budget will not hold much longer.
We've been told the train line will be fixed 'soon.' I give it two years at best. By then half of us will have moved away.
He says he'll change, but I've heard it all before. I don't believe he'll stop gambling, and I can't put my hope in it again. I'm keeping my own account separate, and it hurts to write that.
I think the flowers will die in this frost. I covered them with old sheets, but the cold is supposed to deepen. I won't be surprised to find brown stalks tomorrow.
The football club announced another coaching change. It's the fourth in three years, and I can't see them climbing out of the bottom half. I'm tired of getting my hopes up every August.
I got the scan report but I can't read it. The words look serious, and I expect the doctor to say I need further tests. My mind has already gone to the worst places.
I'm certain our online class will lag again tomorrow. The internet here drops every evening and the provider never fixes it. I'll probably miss half the lecture and I'm already irritated.
With so many applicants for the scholarship, I know I won't be chosen. My marks are decent, not great. I'm filling in the form mostly out of habit.
The old banyan tree leans more each monsoon, and I think the next storm will bring it down. The ward office ignored our letter. I'm afraid it will crush the fence, or worse.
Whenever the department says 'restructuring,' someone loses their job. I'm expecting the same this time, and I suspect I'm near the top of the list. I've started quietly checking job boards, nervous.
The cough is nearly gone, and the pharmacist said the next week should bring a full recovery. I'm already planning to start swimming again. Things are looking up.
I think our little neighbourhood choir has real potential. We were off-key at the start, but last night we nailed the harmony. I'm hopeful we'll be good enough for the winter concert.
Even though my first batch of bread turned into a brick, I can tell I'm getting the hang of it. I'm sure the next loaf will rise properly. I've already bought better yeast.
The bank approved a smaller loan than I asked for, but it's enough to start. I believe the shop will do well in its first year. I'm going to take it.
My daughter's fever dropped overnight, and the doctor said the worst is behind us. I'm hopeful she'll be back at school by Monday. I slept better than I have all week.
The company says new projects are coming in the new year, and the pipeline does look full. I expect a good year ahead for our team. I'm going to plan some leave around spring.
My exam scores are creeping up, one paper at a time. I think I'm on track to get into the course I want. I'm trying not to jinx it, but I feel good about the direction.
Now that the dispute with the neighbour is out in the open, I have a feeling things will improve. We're both too stubborn to stay angry forever. I'll bring over some sweets this weekend.
I put my name down for the marathon next April. I'm slow now, but my training log shows steady progress, and I'm certain I'll finish. It gives me something to look forward to every morning.
The seedlings are tiny, but they look healthy. I'm hopeful for a good harvest if the weather holds. I might even have enough tomatoes to share with the whole building.
We got a decent offer on the old house, and the agent thinks another buyer might come forward. I think we'll sell well before the end of the year. I'm ready to move on.
My project got a lukewarm review, but the mentor said the idea has legs. I think with another month of work it could become something strong. I'm going to push on.
The new bus route starts next week, which should cut my commute in half. I think my mornings will be calmer from now on. I might even have time for a proper breakfast.
Our team is young and raw, but they learn quickly. I believe that by the end of the season they'll be a proper side. I'm looking forward to watching them grow.
After the bad winter, the farmers around here are cautiously upbeat. The early rains came on time, and they expect a decent crop. I hope that holds, and everything points the right way so far.
I've just finished the first chapter of my novel. It's rough, but I like where it's going. I feel sure I'll finish it by summer.
My son says he wants to retake the entrance test, and I think he'll do much better this time. He's studying with real focus. I'm quietly confident.
The weather has turned dry, and I think the road work will finally be completed. The workers have returned and the machines are humming. I might get to cycle on fresh tarmac by November.
I haven't found a job yet, but I've had two interviews this month, which is more than before. I believe an offer is coming. I'm keeping my chin up.
Ever since we changed the shop's layout, more people are stopping by. I think this could be the turnaround we needed. I'm going to try a small sale next week.
Grandma's recovery has been slow but steady. I think she'll be dancing at the family wedding in December. Everyone in the house has started believing it too.
I used to think I'd never pick up drawing, but my lines are getting steadier. I'm convinced a few more months will make a real difference. I bought a better set of pencils today.
The caterer has confirmed the menu and the hall is booked for the family function. I'm sure everything will come together. It might actually go smoothly this time.
I think the quiet in our house will pass. My husband is just stressed with work, and once the quarter ends, we'll be ourselves again. I'm choosing to hope.
The research grant came with fewer funds than we'd hoped, but the team is energised. I believe we can still publish something solid. Every small result so far has pointed the right way.
After months of tension, my brother and I talked for an hour. I don't think everything is mended, but I have a feeling we're heading somewhere better. I'm glad we tried.
The mountain clinic is opening next spring, and I'm sure it will change life for the villages up there. They already have doctors lined up. I might volunteer for a week.
My first attempt at dosa was a mess, but I could tell the batter was nearly right. I think I'll get it with a little practice. I'm trying again tomorrow morning.
I have a gut feeling the audition will go well. I've rehearsed until the lines feel natural. Whatever happens, I think this is the start of something for me, and I can't wait to walk in.
The town's recycling drive has already gathered a good crowd of volunteers. I believe in a year our park will look completely different. I can almost picture it clean.
I found a handwritten note from my late father tucked inside an old book. I froze, not expecting anything of the kind. Reading his familiar scrawl brought a lump to my throat.
I walked into the office and everyone was wearing the same ridiculous hat. I stood in the doorway, baffled, until someone explained it was the result of a bet. I haven't laughed this much in weeks.
The librarian told me the book I'd given up on had been returned, with a pressed flower tucked inside. I was floored for a moment. Who even does that for a stranger?
My phone buzzed with a message from my cousin in Canada saying he was at the airport in my city. I read it four times. He hadn't told a single person he was coming.
I won the raffle at the school fair! I hadn't even remembered buying a ticket, so when they called my name I just sat there. My daughter had to nudge me to go up.
I found out today that my quiet neighbour is a retired national swimmer. Nobody in the building had any idea. I nearly dropped my groceries when the old photograph came up on his screen.
When the postman handed me a parcel from a stranger, I was baffled. Inside was the scarf I left on a train eight months ago. I still don't know how they tracked me down.
I did not expect the film to end the way it did. I gasped out loud in the cinema, and the whole row turned to look at me. I'm still thinking about that last scene.
The water from the tap suddenly turned brown, and I stared at it in disbelief. It had been fine ten minutes earlier. I couldn't stop gagging at the smell, and I called my neighbour to check.
I was shocked when the shy boy in my class delivered a flawless speech. I'd assumed he would stumble through it. The teacher actually applauded, and so did the rest of us.
Out of the blue, my ex sent me a message wishing me luck for my exam. I was stunned. I hadn't heard from him in two years, and I don't know what to make of it.
I opened my locker at the gym and found a hamster sitting inside. Someone must have hidden it there as a joke. I yelped, and the whole corridor turned to stare at me.
I was astonished to see my name in the newspaper this morning for the neighbourhood clean-up. I hadn't known anyone had taken a photograph. My mother cut it out and stuck it to the fridge, beaming.
The shopkeeper knocked a third off the price without my even asking. I'd braced myself for a long bargaining session. I walked out a little dazed and very pleased.
I never thought my grandfather could cook, yet he served a perfect biryani tonight. We all stared at him. He said he'd learned it in the army and just smiled.
A massive crash rattled the windows, and I jumped out of my chair. It was only a lorry shedding its load, but my heart took a while to settle. I never expected that on such a quiet afternoon.
I can't believe how many people showed up to the book reading. I expected five, maybe six, and there were over forty. I had to borrow chairs from the next room.
I was blindsided when my landlord returned the whole deposit, even though I'd scratched the floor. I had made peace with losing half of it. I called twice just to make sure it wasn't an error.
I opened the oven and the cake had risen into a perfect dome. It never does that for me. I stood there laughing, honestly baffled.
The principal asked me, of all people, to give the farewell speech. I had no idea he even knew my name. I said yes before my brain caught up with my mouth.
I was stunned to learn that my friend has been secretly learning sign language for a year. She suddenly began signing at dinner with the deaf couple next door. I'm still amazed.
I woke up to snow this morning in a city where it practically never snows. I stared out of the window for ages in disbelief. The kids are already outside in their pyjamas.
I checked my account and found an extra month of salary credited. I assumed it was an error, but HR confirmed it's a bonus. I'm still gaping at the number.

A stranger on the train started a conversation, and within ten minutes we realised we'd attended the same tiny school. What are the chances? We spent the rest of the journey trading names of teachers.
I caught my reflection in a shop window and didn't recognise myself for a second. When did my hair go that grey? It startled me more than I'd like to admit.
The whole class went quiet when the new teacher began the lesson in verse. I was shocked, then oddly fascinated. I've never seen maths introduced like that before.
I opened the door to find the entire street gathered with a cake for my mother's seventieth birthday. She gasped and clutched my arm. I had no clue the neighbours had planned it.
My little cousin said his first full sentence today, and it was a complaint about vegetables. We all just stared and then burst out laughing. None of us expected it to be so clear.
I found a snake curled on the doorstep at dawn. I froze and held my breath until the gardener took it away. I'm still shaking at the thought of stepping out barefoot.
The test result was the opposite of what I'd expected. I'd braced for failure and instead saw a top score. I asked the teacher to double-check it.
I'm not upset that Maya didn't invite me. I noticed it, shrugged, and moved on with my evening. It was a small thing and I haven't thought about it since.
People say I should be devastated about the move. Mostly I'm busy boxing up books and labelling cables. Maybe the feelings will come later, or maybe they won't.
I thought the farewell would make me cry. Instead I laughed all evening with my old colleagues and felt wonderfully light. It's odd how wrong my prediction was.
My mother is sure I'm angry with her, but I'm not. I was just tired and wanted a quiet afternoon. I'll call her later to tell her so.
I'd expected the audit to terrify me, yet I felt almost nothing walking in. Everything was in order and the auditor was polite. I came out ready for lunch.
Our neighbours assume we're thrilled about the new baby. We are, but we're also scared. I haven't had the courage to say the second part out loud.
My teacher said the others were jealous of my marks, but I didn't sense it. They congratulated me kindly. Whether he was right, I honestly can't tell.
I'm not scared of the dark anymore, but I still leave the hallway light on. Old habits, I suppose. It's just part of the night routine now.
Everyone thought I'd hate the new city. I don't. I find the narrow streets charming, and I've started to enjoy my morning walks. I'd never admit it to my mother yet.
The doctor warned that the medicine could make me anxious. So far it hasn't; I feel the same as always. I'm keeping an eye on it anyway.
Dad says I'm too soft on my younger brother. Maybe, but I'm not annoyed at him, only worried he's drifting away from us. I'd rather keep the door open than argue.
She wrote that she was heartbroken, but her tone read so flat that I wasn't sure. I couldn't tell whether she wanted comfort or space. I haven't answered yet.
I expected to dislike the sambar at the new place, but it was lovely. I went back for seconds and even asked for the recipe. The waiter laughed at me.
My colleague insists the layoffs won't touch our team. I don't share her calm. I can't help picturing the worst, and I told her so gently.
If it rains tomorrow, I'd be disappointed about the picnic, but the forecast looks fine. So for now I'm buying fruit and packing a mat. No sense being gloomy before anything has happened.
They call me brave for speaking up in the meeting, but my knees were shaking. I felt nothing like courage; I felt sick the whole time. Still, I said it.
My friend was ecstatic about her result, and I clapped along with everyone. For me it was an ordinary day, neither good nor bad. I was there to support her.
I'm not sad about the end of the course. I learned what I needed and it's time to go. I'm just curious about what comes next.
My sister assumes I resent her for getting the bigger room. Truthfully I don't care about rooms. What bothers me is that she never asks me anything about my life.
I didn't cry at the funeral, and people kept glancing at me. Grief doesn't arrive on schedule, I suppose. It hit me days later while I was washing a cup.
He said he was sorry, and I know he meant it, but sorry doesn't feel like enough. I'm still resentful and I'm not ready to forgive. I'm going to leave it for a while.
The surgeon said many people feel dizzy after the procedure. I haven't, and I'm eating fine. I'm just noting it down for the follow-up visit.
I thought I'd feel jealous at the reunion, seeing everyone's success. Mostly I felt warm and fond, listening to their stories. It was a nicer evening than I'd braced for.
My neighbour says I should be furious about the noise. I'm not, really; the drilling stops by five and I've learned to work around it. It's a small price for a new building.
Everyone in the family says the hill station was magical. I found it crowded and damp, and I kept waiting to feel what they felt. I never quite did, and that left me a little low.
I'd imagined I would be nervous on stage, but the lights made everything blur away. I felt calm, almost playful. It felt like talking to friends.
My aunt told everyone I'm anxious about the wedding. I'm not. I'm eager for it, and the only nervous person in this house is her.
A colleague asked if the criticism hurt. I said it didn't, and mostly that was true. Late at night, though, I replayed it more than I'd like.
I wouldn't say I was overjoyed to see him, but I wasn't annoyed either. We chatted about the weather and our old street. Then I caught my bus.
They expected me to be thrilled by the surprise trip. Honestly, I was uneasy, because I hate leaving the house unplanned. By the second day I was enjoying it more than I thought I would.
I began the morning irritated by the slow queue at the bank. By noon a stranger had paid for my tea, and my mood lifted completely. I walked home humming.
I was thrilled about the trek until the second day, when the rain turned the trail into a swamp. I was cold and miserable and snapping at my friends. By evening a hot meal had me laughing again.
For weeks I couldn't sleep from worry about the loan. Then the bank restructured it, and I felt a wave of calm. Now I'm planning the shop's reopening with real hope.
We were so happy during the first month in the new flat. Then the leaks began and the landlord ignored every message. I've gone from content to exasperated.
I felt ashamed after forgetting my friend's birthday. She laughed it off and took me out for dinner. I went home soft and warm toward her, and I hugged my mother too.
At first the new baby only made me anxious, and I second-guessed every cry. Now, three months in, I sit and watch her sleep and feel so tender. I don't remember when it changed.

I'd been looking forward to the concert for months and could think of nothing else. When the band cancelled, I just stared at the email, feeling flat. Now I'm looking at refund forms and feel nothing much at all.
I started the week sure I'd fail the driving test. After two good practice sessions, I feel my confidence returning. I think I'll pass this time.
I was furious when my brother sold Dad's old radio. Then he explained he needed the money for tuition, and my anger just drained away. I ended up wishing I'd been the one to help him.
The day was pleasant until I saw the state of the shared kitchen. Mouldy plates, a rotten smell. I felt sick, and the good mood was gone.
I was heartbroken when Biscuit ran away. Two days later the neighbour found him in her garden, filthy but fine. I cried again, but this time from happiness.
I'd looked forward all year to the village fair. When I got there it was half-empty and the rides were broken. I wandered around feeling that the magic had gone.
Before the presentation I felt sick with nerves. Once I began speaking, something relaxed, and I even enjoyed myself. By the end I was grinning like an idiot.
I was dismissive of yoga at first and found it silly. A month later I look forward to the sessions and sleep better. I'm a little embarrassed at how wrong I was.
When the results were delayed, I felt tense and short-tempered with everyone. Then the call came, and I laughed so hard I got hiccups. Now I'm just worn out and very pleased.
I used to love Sunday dinners at Uncle's house. Since the argument over the land, I dread going. Last week the old warmth was gone, and I left early with a heavy feeling.
I woke up excited for my first day at the new school. By lunchtime nobody had spoken to me, and I felt small and invisible. In the evening a girl waved, and I let myself hope tomorrow will be better.
I assumed the trip would be a disaster after we missed the first train. But the detour took us through a market I'd never have found, and I ended up delighted. I'd happily miss a train again.
The farewell dinner began with laughter and old stories. Midway, someone mentioned the empty chair, and I felt my throat close. I stayed quiet for the rest of the evening.
I resented the extra shifts at first and complained to everyone. Slowly I realised I was learning faster than ever, and now I actually enjoy the hard assignments. My boss noticed it before I did.
My fear of deep water has eased since I started lessons. In the beginning I could hardly step into the pool, and now I'm floating without help. I'm proud and a bit giddy.
I was thrilled by the idea of the road trip, but two days in I'm sick of the car and my cousin's playlist. Sitting here at a roadside dhaba, I feel irritable and ready for home.
We were close friends until the argument last spring. I miss her a lot, but I also feel a quiet anger whenever I think about what she said. I haven't decided whether to call.
I felt sure the job would be a nightmare, and the first week was awful. Then my colleague quietly showed me the ropes, and I started to believe it could work out. I'm cautiously hopeful now.
Before the wedding I was on edge, sure something would go wrong. When the ceremony ended without a hitch, I laughed and cried in the same minute. Now I just feel full.
I was proud of my garden until the caterpillars came. Now I stand there every morning, disgusted by the holes in the leaves and expecting to lose it all.
Mum seemed so frail after the operation that I was terrified. A week later she was scolding me about my shoes, and I could finally breathe. I'm so glad to hear her nagging again.
I was bored through most of the lecture. Then the speaker began telling a story about her time at sea, and I sat up. Now I want to read everything she's written.
I came in confident about the match but we lost badly. I felt crushed for an hour, then went out for tea with the team and began to feel better. Next time we'll train harder.
I was nervous about the new neighbours, expecting trouble. They brought over sweets and fixed our gate latch without being asked. I'm starting to feel quite at home on this street.
Woke up at half past five and did some stretching. Packed a lunch of rice and curd, then caught the 6:50 train. The compartment was crowded but I found a seat near the window.
I spent the evening reorganising my bookshelf by subject. Moved the cookbooks to the lower shelf and the manuals to the top. It took about two hours.
The plumber came at eleven and replaced the washer in the kitchen tap. He charged four hundred rupees. I wiped the counter afterward and put the tools of his trade back where they were.
Went to the weekly market and bought tomatoes, spinach, and a kilo of lentils. Stopped at the stationery shop for a refill. Then I walked home along the canal path.
Today's class covered the water cycle and a few review questions on it. We copied a diagram into our notebooks. Homework is two paragraphs on evaporation.
Our building's water supply is off between ten and one on Tuesdays. I filled two buckets in advance and did the dishes early. The tank was refilled around two.
Updated my resume and saved it as a PDF. Then I sent it to two recruiters and filed the confirmation emails in a folder. I'll check for replies on Thursday.
Took the dog out at seven and again at nine. Washed the bowls and swept the front steps. Afterward I watched the evening news.
Had a call with the electricity board about the meter reading. They said a technician would visit within the week. I wrote the complaint number on the fridge calendar.
I cooked dal, rice and a simple cabbage curry for dinner. Washed up and wiped down the stove afterward. Then I read the paper for half an hour.
Cycled to the community library and borrowed two novels and a gardening guide. The librarian stamped the due date as the twelfth. I rode back before it got dark.
Worked on the quarterly report from nine until about one. Had lunch at my desk and emailed the draft to my manager. The afternoon went to filing and a short call with the vendor.
Did the monthly grocery order online and set the delivery for Saturday morning. Also renewed my bus pass and paid the broadband bill. That's the admin done for now.
The yoga class ran for an hour, starting with breathing exercises and ending with a short rest. I rolled up my mat and walked home. Dinner was soup and toast.
Spent Sunday afternoon at the park with my notebook, sketching the old fountain. A few families came and went. I left around five when the light started to fade.
My cousin dropped by with a box of mangoes from the farm. We had tea and talked about his work and the train timings. He left before it got dark.
Took my laptop to the repair shop to replace the battery. The technician said it would be ready in three days. I picked up a mouse pad from the shop next door.
Joined the fortnightly neighbourhood call about rubbish pickup times. Minutes were taken, and the next meeting is set for the thirtieth. I noted the new schedule in my planner.
Practised my French vocabulary for thirty minutes using flash cards. Then I listened to a short podcast during dinner. Tomorrow's focus is verbs in the past tense.
We left for the temple at eight and reached by half past nine. Queued for about forty minutes, offered flowers, and had prasad before heading back. Home by noon.
